newsitem.title: USA: Clinton sets off on seven-state campaign swing.
newsitem.headline: Clinton sets off on seven-state campaign swing.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Sunday began a seven-state campaign trip designed to protect his comfortable lead in key states and expand it in hostile territory.

Before leaving Washington, Clinton announced a $30 million increase in funding for research into the genetics of breast cancer, the creation of an Internet web site on the disease and the establishment of an "Office of Cancer Survivorship" to study issues of concern to survivors of all cancers.
"These steps help us to put science at the service of our families and say we will do whatever it takes to continue the fight until there is a cure for cancer," Clinton said.

The White House said the $30 million was being shifted from other parts of the budget -- $20 million from an existing Defense Department breast cancer reseach fund and $10 million from a National Institutes of Health medical research fund.

The initiatives, announced in the White House Rose Garden, seemed designed to show Clinton in a presidential light and to court women voters, who have shown a durable preference for Clinton over his Republican opponent Bob Dole.
The president then turned his attention to raw politics by traveling to Virginia, a state that has not voted to send a Democrat to the White House since 1964 when it went for Lyndon Johnson.

Clinton was also to travel to Nashville, Tennessee, making his fourth visit to the state since August in an effort to ensure that Vice President Al Gore did not suffer the embarrassment of losing his home state.
There seemed little danger of that, as a recent Tennessee opinion poll gave Clinton a 15 percentage point lead over Dole, but the Clinton-Gore campaign was taking no chances.

With double-digit leads in most national opinion polls -- a Reuters tracking poll released on Sunday put him ahead of Dole by 13.4 percentage points -- Clinton appeared to be playing a complex campaign endgame.
On one hand he sought to buttress his commanding position in traditionally crucial Midwestern states like Illinois and Ohio, which he will visit on Monday and Tuesday.

On the other, given this very strength, he wanted to use the campaign's waning days to further objectives beyond his own re-election -- like positioning Gore for a run at the White House in 2000 and helping Democratic congressional candidates.

During a fleeting afternoon visit to Springfield, Virginia, Clinton was scheduled to campaign alongside Mark Warner, a Democratic businessman seeking to oust the 18-year Republican John Warner from the Senate.

While recent polls gave Clinton a six to nine point lead over Dole in Virginia -- recently one of the most reliably Republican states -- an Oct. 11-12 survey showed Mark Warner trailing by 12 points, 48-36.

Clinton was to move to Missouri, a bellwether state in presidential elections, where he holds a slender, four-point margin, according to a Mason-Dixon Political/Media Research poll taken Oct. 14-16, which put him ahead of Dole 44-40.
On Monday Clinton was scheduled to make speaches in St. Louis, Minneapolis and Chicago and on Tuesday in Columbus, Ohio and Philadelphia.

After a one-night stopover at White House, Clinton was to begin a a seven-day campaign blitz taking him across the country and ending in Little Rock, Arkansas, for election night -- near the site where he declared in candidacy in October 1991.
